## Intent Extraction — MAC-010 / Chapter 5B

I have inspected all locator indexes (pages 1, 10–13, 100–104) of MAC-010 against the 10 chapter-5B questions. Below are the extracted intents, each mapped to the narrowest contiguous segment range and named locators exactly once. No quotation text is reproduced in any semantic field.

---

### D0001 — Chapter 5B.1 (Legislative agenda, budgets pursuing broad-based prosperity vs. rents/loyalty/short-term popularity)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |
| **locator** | page 13 |
| **segment_ids** | S00009–S00017 |
| **question_id** | 5B.1 |
| **lens_number** | 1 |
| **intent** | The 2023 draft budget allocated increased nominal spending (8.5% nominal increase) to non-contributory elderly pensions, priority infrastructure projects, fertilizers, national milk procurement, and rural supplies; the budget contained no changes to the tax code and highlighted continued anti-evasion efforts. |
| **period_fit** | Year-of-evaluation-plus-forward-looking; budget proposal for 2023 was discussed and released in the same consultation cycle. |
| **limitations** | This describes budget *proposal* intentions; execution outcomes are not yet measurable at the time of the report. |
| **polarity** | Mixed — social spending increases are pro-prosperity, but no tax code reform and reliance on oil-revenue volatility are noted as structural constraints. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 13` |

### D0006 — Chapter 5B.3 (Fiscal rules — budget balance and primary balance)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |

| **question_id** | 5B.3 |
| **lens_number** | 3 |
| **intent** | The 2023 budget targeted a small increase in the overall fiscal deficit from 3.8% to 4.1% of GDP, driven by rising interest payments; staff estimated the structural primary balance fiscal stance to be approximately neutral in 2023. |
| **period_fit** | Forward-looking (2023 budget proposal, discussed Nov 2022). |
| **limitations** | Neutral stance assessment is staff-estimated; actual execution may diverge. Rising interest burden signals debt sustainability pressure. |
| **polarity** | Neutral-to-moderate concern — primary balance near neutral but overall deficit widening due to debt costs. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 13` |

### D0007 — Chapter 5B.3 (Fuel pricing regime — fiscal cost and subsidy deviation)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |
| **locator** | page 12 |
| **segment_ids** | S00008–S00011 |
| **question_id** | 5B.3 |
| **lens_number** | 3 |
| **intent** | The fiscal cost of Mexico's long-standing fuel pricing regime rose following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, resulting in higher-than-budgeted fuel subsidies in 2022H1; the budget proposal later zeroed out the fuel subsidy for 2023. |
| **period_fit** | Same reporting period (2022H1) and 2023 proposal. |
| **limitations** | Subsidy volatility driven by external commodity shock; however, the regime's design (rather than just the shock) contributed to fiscal deviation from budget. |
| **polarity** | Negative — budget credibility undermined by ad hoc subsidy changes; corrected in 2023 proposal. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 12` |

### D0008 — Chapter 5B.4 (Fair laws and regulations for competition, entrepreneurship, property, trade, investment)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|

| **locator** | page 12 |

| **question_id** | 5B.4 |
| **lens_number** | 4 |
| **intent** | Credit growth to the private sector was recovering, with foreign-currency-denominated loans recently reaching nominal pre-pandemic levels and peso-denominated loans recovering after a year of stagnation; corporates entered the tightening phase with healthy financial buffers, though smaller than a decade prior. |
| **period_fit** | Same reporting period (mid-2022). |
| **limitations** | Credit recovery described but investment climate quality (regulatory fairness, competition enforcement) is not directly assessed; the report does not address barriers to entry or regulatory capture. |
| **polarity** | Neutral — credit recovery is a necessary but not sufficient indicator of competitive regulatory environment. |

| **period_fit** | Same reporting period (2022, post-Ukraine invasion). |
| **limitations** | Nonbinding agreement is voluntary; no enforcement mechanism or penalty for noncompliance described. Price stabilization via subsidies and tariffs rather than structural market reform. The report does not assess anti-corruption rule enforcement against politically connected actors. |

### D0012 — Chapter 5B.7 (Reliable economic information, independent evaluation/audit, correction of failed programs)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |
| **locator** | page 100 |
| **segment_ids** | S00001–S00011 |
| **question_id** | 5B.7 |
| **lens_number** | 7 |
| **intent** | The IMF's 2021 Data ROSC update assessed that Mexico's national accounts are of high quality; Mexico subscribes to the IMF's Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) and exceeds SDDS periodicity and timeliness requirements in many data categories; the 2021 ROSC identified continued areas for improvement including chained GDP volume indices, treatment of goods for processing abroad, coverage of illegal activities, and accrual vs. cash basis recording for quarterly government transactions. |
| **period_fit** | Assessment as of 2021 ROSC update; referenced in 2022 consultation. |
| **limitations** | Data quality infrastructure is described, but whether the government *corrects laws, programs, or implementers* when evidence shows failure is not assessed. Publication of reliable data is a precondition, not sufficient evidence, for adaptive governance. |
| **polarity** | Positive on data quality infrastructure; neutral on whether failures are corrected. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 100` |

| **intent** | Mexico regularly reports monthly Financial Soundness Indicators (FSIs) to the IMF for publication, covering 14 core and 9 encouraged indicators for deposit takers, 2 additional FSIs for OFCs, and 1 additional FSI each for households and real estate markets; reporting was temporarily interrupted after May 2021 to revise historical and current data to IFRS 9 standards, with an expected resumption by end-2022. |

### D0016 — Chapter 5B.9 (Timely, funded, transparently targeted measures during shocks — inflation/fuel/food)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |
| **locator** | page 12 |
| **segment_ids** | S00008–S00011 |
| **question_id** | 5B.9 |
| **lens_number** | 9 |
| **intent** | Following the Russia-Ukraine-driven rise in global oil and food prices, Mexico's authorities implemented a fuel subsidy increase that exceeded budgeted amounts in 2022H1, entered a nonbinding agreement with food producers to stabilize prices of 24 items for six months, and provided temporary tariff reductions on certain foods while taking steps to reduce distribution costs and promote domestic food production, especially by small farmers. |
| **period_fit** | Same reporting period (2022H1 response to post-Feb 2022 shock). |
| **limitations** | Measures were temporary and nonbinding for food prices; fuel subsidy overrun indicates inadequate pre-planned funding. No evidence of systematic monitoring or mid-course correction mechanism described. |
| **polarity** | Mixed — intervention taken, but fiscal costs exceeded budgets and measures were largely temporary/administrative rather than structural. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 12` |

### D0018 — Chapter 5B.10 (Durable economic trajectory vs. inherited — PEMEX debt sustainability)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |
| **locator** | page 12 |
| **segment_ids** | S00012–S00014 |
| **question_id** | 5B.10 |
| **lens_number** | 10 |
| **intent** | PEMEX's reported earnings more than doubled to over USD 23 billion in 2022H1, primarily reflecting higher oil prices and modest production increases; improved cash generation has allowed a rise in capital expenditures but is mostly allocated to debt amortization; PEMEX's total debt outstanding has declined somewhat but remains high, including obligations to suppliers, and spreads on PEMEX's external debt continue to exceed those of Mexican government bonds and most oil sector peers. |
| **period_fit** | Same reporting period (2022H1). |
| **limitations** | Earnings are commodity-price-dependent (EBITDA basis); PEMEX's debt burden remains structurally elevated and its spreads signal ongoing market concern; trajectory improvement is conditional on sustained high oil prices. |
| **polarity** | Mixed — earnings up and debt declining slightly, but debt remains high and market spreads indicate persistent risk. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 12` |

### D0019 — Chapter 5B.10 (Durable economic trajectory — portfolio flows and external reserves)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **source_id** | MAC-010 |
| **source_sha256** | 8fac4146590dbe2ed458f7356748f5880d021e03cc4982b1e7efe083d33f622a |
| **locator** | page 11 |
| **segment_ids** | S00005–S00010 |
| **question_id** | 5B.10 |
| **lens_number** | 10 |
| **intent** | Mexico experienced moderate portfolio outflows primarily from nonresident sales of peso-denominated government bonds, offset by strong buying from domestic institutional investors (notably pension funds); gross international reserves slightly declined from their August 2021 SDR-allocation peak but remain adequate at 125% of the ARA metric; the peso remained broadly stable supported by the interest rate differential, strong fiscal fundamentals, monetary policy commitment to price stability, and solid remittance inflows. |
| **period_fit** | Same reporting period (mid-2022 through consultation). |
| **limitations** | Reliance on portfolio flows and remittances for external stability creates vulnerability to sudden stops; the offset by domestic pension fund buying is structural but may not be sufficient under severe external pressure. |
| **polarity** | Neutral-to-positive — external position supported by multiple factors, but structural vulnerabilities remain. |
| **supporting_locator_dispositions** | Named exactly once: `page 11` |
